readings.c2s1:
¶
'''virtuefy''' (vėr′t̮ū-fī), ''v. t.''; pret. and pp. ''virtuefied'', ppr. ''virtuefying''. [< ''virtue'' + ''-fy''.] To give virtue to; impart the quality of virtue to. [Rare.]
{{smaller block|It is this which ''virtuefies'' emotion, even though there be nothing virtuous which is not voluntary.
{{right|''Chalmers'', Constitution of Man, ii. (''Encyc. Dict.'')}}}}

'''virtueless''' (vėr′t̮ū-les), ''a.'' [< ''virtue'' + ''-less''.] Destitute of virtue, potency, or efficacy; worthless.
{{smaller block|<poem>And these digressive things
Are such as you may well endure, since (being deriv’d from kings,
And kings not poor nor ''virtueless'') you cannot hold me base,
Nor scorn my words, which oft, though true, in mean men meet disgrace.</poem>
{{right|''Chapman'', Iliad, xiv. 107.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>''Virtueless'' she wish’d all herbs and charms,
Wherewith false men increase their patients’ harms.</poem>
{{right|''Fairfax''.}}}}
{{smaller block|On the right hand of one of the marines of Salvator, in the Pitti palace, there is a passage of sea reflecting the sunrise, which is thoroughly good, and very like Turner; the rest of the picture, as the one opposite to it, utterly ''virtueless''.
{{right|''Ruskin'', Mod. Painters, II. v. 1.}}}}

'''virtue-proof†''' (vėr′t̮ū-pröf), ''a.'' Irresistible in virtue.
{{smaller block|<poem>No veil
She needed, ''virtue-proof''; no thought infirm
Alter’d her cheek.</poem>
{{right|''Milton'', P. L., v. 384.}}}}

'''virtuosa''' (vir-tö-ō′sä), ''n.''; pl. ''virtuose'' (-se). [It.: see ''virtuoso''.] The feminine of ''virtuoso''.
{{smaller block|A fine concert, in which La Diamantina, a famous ''virtuosa'', played on the violin divinely, and sung angelically.
{{right|''Gray'', Letters, I. 76.}}}}

'''virtuose''' (vir-tọ̈-ōs′), ''a.'' [< It. ''virtuoso'': see ''virtuoso''.] Same as ''virtuosic''.
readings.c3s3:
{{smaller block|<poem>
The ladies sought around
For ''virtuous'' herbs, which, gather’d from the ground,
They squeez’d the juice and cooling ointment made.
</poem>
{{right|''Dryden'', Flower and Leaf, l. 418.}}}}
='''Syn. 2''' and '''3.''' Upright, exemplary, worthy, righteous. See ''morality''.

'''virtuously''' (vėr′tṳ̄-us-li), ''adv.'' In a virtuous manner; in conformity with the moral law or with duty; chastely; honorably.
{{smaller block|The gods are my witnesses I desire to do ''virtuously''.
{{right|''Sir P. Sidney.''}}
I knew you lov’d her, ''virtuously'' you lov’d her.
{{right|''Beau. and Fl.'', Knight of Malta, ii. 2.}}
<poem>
And I’ll be your true servant,
Ever from this hour ''virtuously'' to love you,
Chastely and modestly to look upon you.
</poem>
{{right|''Fletcher'', Rule a Wife, v. 5.}}}}

'''virtuousness''' (vėr′tṳ̄-us-nes), ''n.'' [Early mod. E. also ''vertuousnes''; < ''virtuous'' + ''-ness''.] The state or character of being virtuous.
{{smaller block|Polemon . . . from thensforthe becam a Phi’er [philosopher] of singular gravitee, of incomparable sobrenes, of moste constante ''vertuousnes'', and so contynued all his lif aftir.
{{right|''Udall'' (Ellis’s Lit. Letters, p. 6).}}
The love of Britomart, . . . the ''vertuousnes'' of Belphœbe.
{{right|''Spenser'', To Raleigh. Prefix to F. Q.}}}}

'''virulence''' (vir′ọ̈-le̤ns), ''n.'' [< F. ''virulence'' = Sp. Pg. ''virulencia'' = It. ''virulenza'', < LL. ''virulentia'', an offensive odor, < L. ''virulentus'', full of poison: see ''virulent''.] The quality of being virulent, or charged with virus. {{smaller|(''a'') The quality or property of being extremely acrimonious or poisonous: as, the ''viru-''}}

<noinclude><pagequality level="1" user="transcriber" />{{RunningHeader|virtue|6767|virulence}}</noinclude>{{nop}}{{smaller block|In euerie degree and sort of men ''vertue'' is commendable, but not egally: not onely because mens estates are vnegall, but for that also ''vertue'' it selfe is not in euery respect of egall value and estimation.
{{right|''Puttenham'', Arte of Eng. Poesie, p. 34.}}}}

{{smaller block|He daub’d his vice with show of ''virtue.''
{{right|''Shak.'', Rich. III., iii. 5. 29.}}}}

{{smaller block|If ''Virtue'' be to itself no small Reward, and Vice in a great measure its own Punishment, we have a solid ground to go upon.
{{right|''Shaftesbury'', Moralists, ii. § 3.}}}}

{{smaller block|To do good for its own sake is ''virtue'', to do it for some ulterior end or object, not itself good, is never ''virtue;'' and never to act but for the sake of an end, other than doing well and right, is the mark of vice.
{{right|''F. H. Bradley'', Ethical Studies, p. 56.}}}}

{{smaller block|Hutcheson, who is the very founder in modern times of the doctrine of “a moral sense,” and who has defended the disinterested character of ''virtue'' more powerfully than perhaps any other moralist, resolved all ''virtue'' into benevolence, or the pursuit of the happiness of others; but he maintained that the excellence and obligation of benevolence are revealed to us by “a moral sense.”
{{right|''Lecky'', Europ. Morals, I. 4.}}}}

'''3.''' A particular moral excellence: as, the ''virtue'' of temperance or of charity.
{{smaller block|<poem>For, if our ''virtues''
Did not go forth of us, ’twere all alike
As if we had them not.</poem>
{{right|''Shak.'', M. for M., i. 1. 34.}}}}

{{smaller block|Being a Prince so full of ''Virtues'', . . . he [the Black Prince] left no Place for any Vice.
{{right|''Baker'', Chronicles, p. 127.}}}}

{{smaller block|The ''virtues'' of a private Christian are patience, obedience, submission, and the like; but those of a magistrate, or general, or a king, are prudence, counsel, active fortitude, coercive power, awful command, and the exercise of magnanimity as well as justice.
{{right|''Dryden'', Orig. and Prog. of Satire.}}}}

{{smaller block|Great faults, therefore, may grow out of great ''virtues'' in excess.
{{right|''De Quincey'', Style, i.}}}}

'''4.''' Specifically, female purity; chastity.
{{smaller block|Angelo had never the purpose to corrupt her; only he hath made an essay of her ''virtue''.
{{right|''Shak.'', M. for M., iii. 1. 164.}}}}
{{smaller block|''Hast.'' I believe the girl has ''virtue''.
''Mar.'' And if she has, I should be the last man in the world that would attempt to corrupt it.
{{right|''Goldsmith'', She Stoops to Conquer, iv.}}}}

'''5.''' Any good quality, merit, or admirable faculty.
{{smaller block|The times which followed the Restoration peculiarly require that unsparing impartiality which is his [Hallam’s] most distinguishing ''virtue''.
{{right|''Macaulay'', Hallam’s Const. Hist.}}}}
{{smaller block|The ''virtue'' of books is to be readable, and of orators to be interesting. {{right|''Emerson'', Eloquence.}}}}

'''6.''' An inherent power; a property capable of producing certain effects; strength; force; potency; efficacy; influence, especially active influence, and often medicinal efficacy.
{{smaller block|Zif zou lyke to knowe the ''Vertues'' of the Dyamand (as men may fynde in the Lipidarye, that many men knowen noght), I schalle telle zou. {{right|''Mandeville'', Travels, p. 159.}}}}
{{smaller block|This Salomon was wise and knew the ''vertues'' of stones and trees, and so hee knew the course of the starres.
{{right|''Sir T. Malory'', Morte d’Arthur, III. lxxxvi.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>I see there ’s ''virtue'' in my heavenly words.</poem>
{{right|''Marlowe'', Faustus, i. 3.}}}}
{{smaller block|Jesus, immediately knowing that ''virtue'' had gone out of him, turned him about in the press, and said, Who touched my clothes? {{right|Mark v. 30.}}}}
{{smaller block|Your If is the only peace-maker; much ''virtue'' in If.
{{right|''Shak.'', As you Like it, v. 4. 108.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>These I can cure, such secret ''virtue'' lies
In herbs applièd by a virgin’s hand.</poem>
{{right|''Fletcher'', Faithful Shepherdess, i. 1.}}}}

'''7.''' One of the orders of the celestial hierarchy. The virtues are often represented in art as angels in complete armor, bearing pennons and battle-axes.
{{smaller block|<poem>Hear, all ye angels, progeny of light,
Thrones, dominations, princedoms, ''virtues'', powers!
Hear my decree.</poem>
{{right|''Milton'', P. L., v. 601.}}}}
'''8†.''' A mighty work; a miracle.
{{smaller block|Thanne Jhesus bigan to seye repreef to citees in whiche ful manye ''vertues'' of him weren doon. {{right|''Wyclif'', Mat. xi. 20.}}}}
'''By virtue of, in virtue of''', {{smaller|by or through the power, force, efficacy, or authority of.}}
{{smaller block|''By vertu of'' the auctorite that he hath of the chirche.
{{right|''Merlin'' (E. E. T. S.), i. 21.}}
The king then assumed the power ''in virtue of'' his prerogative. {{right|''D. Webster'', Speech, March 10, 1818.}}}}
'''Cardinal virtues.''' {{smaller|See ''cardinal''.—}}'''Material virtue†.''' {{smaller|See ''material''.—}}'''Moral virtue.''' {{smaller|See ''moral''.—}}'''Theological virtues,''' {{smaller|the three virtues faith, hope, and charity.—}}'''The seven chief''' {{smaller|or}} '''principal virtues.''' {{smaller|See ''seven''.—}}'''To make a virtue of necessity,''' {{smaller|to do as if from inclination or sense of duty what has to be done by compulsion.}}
{{smaller block|However, we were forced to ''make a virtue of necessity'', and humour him, for it was neither time nor place to be angry with the Indians, all our lives lying in their hand.
{{right|''Dampier'', Voyages, I. 13.}}}}
{{smaller|='''Syn. 2.''' ''Morals'', ''Ethics'', etc. (see ''morality''); probity, integrity, rectitude, worth.}}

'''virtued''' (vėr′tūd), ''a.'' [< ''virtue'' + ''-ed''<sup>2</sup>.] Endued with power or virtue; efficacious.
{{smaller block|<poem>But hath the ''virtu’d'' steel a pow’r to move?
Or can the untouch’d needle point alike?</poem>
{{right|''Quarles'', Emblems, v. 4.}}}}

'''virtuefy''' (vėr′t̮ū-fī), ''v. t.''; pret. and pp. ''virtuefied'', ppr. ''virtuefying''. [< ''virtue'' + ''-fy''.] To give virtue to; impart the quality of virtue to. [Rare.]
{{smaller block|It is this which ''virtuefies'' emotion, even though there be nothing virtuous which is not voluntary.
{{right|''Chalmers'', Constitution of Man, ii. (''Encyc. Dict.'')}}}}

'''virtueless''' (vėr′t̮ū-les), ''a.'' [< ''virtue'' + ''-less''.] Destitute of virtue, potency, or efficacy; worthless.
{{smaller block|<poem>And these digressive things
Are such as you may well endure, since (being deriv’d from kings,
And kings not poor nor ''virtueless'') you cannot hold me base,
Nor scorn my words, which oft, though true, in mean men meet disgrace.</poem>
{{right|''Chapman'', Iliad, xiv. 107.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>''Virtueless'' she wish’d all herbs and charms,
Wherewith false men increase their patients’ harms.</poem>
{{right|''Fairfax''.}}}}
{{smaller block|On the right hand of one of the marines of Salvator, in the Pitti palace, there is a passage of sea reflecting the sunrise, which is thoroughly good, and very like Turner; the rest of the picture, as the one opposite to it, utterly ''virtueless''.
{{right|''Ruskin'', Mod. Painters, II. v. 1.}}}}

'''virtue-proof†''' (vėr′t̮ū-pröf), ''a.'' Irresistible in virtue.
{{smaller block|<poem>No veil
She needed, ''virtue-proof''; no thought infirm
Alter’d her cheek.</poem>
{{right|''Milton'', P. L., v. 384.}}}}

'''virtuosa''' (vir-tö-ō′sä), ''n.''; pl. ''virtuose'' (-se). [It.: see ''virtuoso''.] The feminine of ''virtuoso''.
{{smaller block|A fine concert, in which La Diamantina, a famous ''virtuosa'', played on the violin divinely, and sung angelically.
{{right|''Gray'', Letters, I. 76.}}}}

'''virtuose''' (vir-tọ̈-ōs′), ''a.'' [< It. ''virtuoso'': see ''virtuoso''.] Same as ''virtuosic''. {{smaller block|Mme. Carreno is essentially a ''virtuose'' player, and it was in pieces by Liszt that she astonished her audience.
{{right|''The Academy'', May 17, 1890, p. 346.}}}}

'''virtuosi''', ''n.'' Italian plural of ''virtuoso''.

'''virtuosic''' (vir-tộ-ō′sik), ''a.'' [< ''virtuose'' + ''-ic''.] Exhibiting the artistic qualities and skill of a virtuoso. [Rare.]
{{smaller block|Of late we have had only fugitive pieces of the romantic, and even ''virtuosic'', schools.
{{right|''The Academy'', April 13, 1889, p. 261.}}}}

'''virtuosity''' (vir-tộ-os′i̤-ti), ''n.'' [< ''virtuoso'' + ''-ity''.] '''1.''' Lovers of the elegant arts collectively; the virtuosi.
{{smaller block|It was Zum Grünen Ganse, . . . where all the ''Virtuosity'' and nearly all the Intellect of the place assembled of an evening.
{{right|''Carlyle'', Sartor Resartus, i. 3.}}}}
'''2.''' In the ''fine arts'', exceptional skill; highly cultivated dexterity; thorough control of technic. {{smaller|Virtuosity is really a condition to the highest artistic success, since it means a complete mastery of the materials and processes at the artist’s disposal; but, inasmuch as the ready use of materials and processes is often in itself wonderful to the percipient, virtuosity is often erroneously cultivated and applauded for its own sake. The term is especially applied to music.}}
{{smaller block|In this [inlaid work], as in the later work of most styles of art, mechanical ''virtuosity'' . . . was beginning to usurp the place of originality and purity of design.
{{right|''G. C. M. Birdwood'', Indian Arts, II. 44.}}
This gave to both performers a legitimate opportunity of displaying their ''virtuosity''.
{{right|''The Academy'', June 15, 1889, p. 420.}}
Brilliancy of technique is now the property of nearly every public performer, and instrumental music is being threatened by that decadence which all art history proves is the constant companion of ''virtuosity''.
{{right|''The Century'', XXXV. 2.}}}}

'''virtuoso''' (vir-tọ̈-ō′sō), ''n.''; pl. ''virtuosos, virtuosi'' (-sōz, -si). [= F. ''virtuose'', < It. ''virtuoso'', a virtuoso, lit. one who is excellent, i. e. excels in taste: see ''virtuous.''] '''1†.''' An experimental philosopher; a student of things by direct observation. ''Boyle.''—'''2.''' One who has an instructed appreciation of artistic excellence; a person skilled in or having a critical taste for any of the elegant arts, as painting, sculpture, etc.; one having special knowledge or skill in antiquities, curiosities, and the like.
{{smaller block|The Italians call a man a ''virtuoso'' who loves the noble arts and is a critic in them.
{{right|''Dryden'', On Dufresnoy’s Art of Painting.}}
Our host . . . had been a Colonel in France; . . . was a true old blade, and had been a very curious ''virtuoso'', as we found by a handsome collection of books, medals, . . . and other antiquities. {{right|''Evelyn'', Diary, March 23, 1646.}}
Nothing can be pleasanter than to see a circle of these ''virtuosos'' about a cabinet of medals, descanting upon the value, rarity, and authenticalness of the several pieces that lie before them. {{right|''Addison'', Ancient Medals, i.}}
If this ''virtuoso'' excels in one thing more than another, it is in canes. {{right|''Steele'', Tatler, No. 142.}}
His house, indeed, would not much attract the admiration of the ''virtuoso.'' He built it himself, and it is remarkable only for its plainness. {{right|''Fielding'', Amelia, iii. 12.}}}}
'''3.''' One who is a master of the mechanical part of a fine art, especially music, and who makes display of his dexterity. See ''virtuosity'', 2.

{{smaller block|The ''virtuoso'' afterwards exhibited his marvellous execution in solos by Paganini and Wieniawski.
{{right|''The Academy'', June 1, 1889, p. 386.}}}}

'''virtuosoship''' (vir-tọ̈-ō′sọ̄-ship), ''n.'' [< ''virtuoso'' + ''-ship''.] The occupation or pursuits of a virtuoso. ''Bp. Hurd.''

'''virtuous''' (vėr′t̮ū-us), ''a.'' [Early mod. E. also ''vertuous''; < ME. ''vertuous'', < OF. ''vertuous'', ''vertueux'', F. ''vertueux'' = Sp. Pg. It. ''virtuoso'', virtuous, excellent, effective, efficacious, < LL. ''virtuosus'', good, virtuous, < L. ''virtus'', excellence, virtue: see ''virtue''.] '''1†.''' Having or exhibiting manly strength and courage; valorous; brave; gallant.
{{smaller block|Neuertheles whan Merlin saugh the Saisnes so ''vertouse'', he ascride the kynge Ban: “Sir, what do ye now? ye myght haue hem putte oute of the place longe seth, ffor ye be moo peple be that oon half than thi be.”
{{right|''Merlin'' (E. E. T. S.), iii. 595.}}
<poem>Must all men that are ''virtuous''
Think suddenly to match themselves with me?
I conquer’d him, and bravely; did I not?</poem>
{{right|''Beau. and Fl.'', King and No King, i. 1.}}}}
'''2.''' Possessed of or exhibiting virtue; morally good; acting in conformity with right; discharging moral duties and obligations, and abstaining from immoral practices: as, a ''virtuous'' man.
{{smaller block|A Man of excellent Parts of Body, and of no less Endowments of Mind; valiant and witty; to which if we might add ''vertuous'', he had been compleat.
{{right|''Baker'', Chronicles, p. 107.}}
It is the interest of the world that ''virtuous'' men should attain to greatness, because it gives them the power of doing good.
{{right|''Dryden'', Amboyna, Ded.}}}}

{{smaller block|A ''virtuous'' mind cannot long esteem a base one.
{{right|''Hamilton'', To Miss Schuyler (Works, I. 187).}}}}
{{smaller block|Indeed, as Aristotle says, our idea of a ''virtuous'' man includes the characteristic that he takes pleasure in doing virtuous actions. ''H. Sidgwick'', Methods of Ethics, p. 32.}}

'''3.''' Being in conformity to the moral or divine law: as, a ''virtuous'' deed; a ''virtuous'' life.
{{smaller block|If what we call virtue be only ''virtuous'' because it is useful, it can only be ''virtuous'' when it is useful.
{{right|''Lecky'', Europ. Morals, I. 45.}}}}
{{smaller block|The beauty of a ''virtuous'' action may be explained as consisting in its relation to the ''virtuous'' character in which it has its source, or to the other acts of a ''virtuous'' life, or to the general condition of a ''virtuous'' state of society.
{{right|''Fowler'', Shaftesbury and Hutcheson, p. 67.}}}}
{{smaller block|If there is any ''virtuous'' action performed at any time, that in it which constitutes it ''virtuous'' is the motive of universal love which is its impelling force.
{{right|''Bibliotheca Sacra'', XLVII. 570.}}}}

'''4.''' Chaste; pure; modest.
{{smaller block|Mistress Ford, . . . the modest wife, the ''virtuous'' creature, that hath the jealous fool to her husband.
{{right|''Shak.'', M. W. of W., iv. 2. 136.}}
<poem>Her beauty was beyond compare,
She was both ''virtuous'' and fair.</poem>
{{right|''The Suffolk Miracle'' (Child’s Ballads, I. 218).}}}}

'''5†.''' Efficacious by inherent qualities; having singular or eminent properties or powers; potent; effective.
{{smaller block|<poem>Ther nas no man nowhere so ''vertuous'';
He was the beste beggere in his hous.</poem>
{{right|''Chaucer'', Gen. Prol. to C. T., l. 251.}}}}
{{smaller block|This priuytee is so ''vertuous'' that the vertu therof may not al be declarid.
{{right|''Book of Quinte Essence'' (ed. Furnivall), p. 8.}}
<poem>Culling from every flower
The ''virtuous'' sweets. ''Shak.'', 2 Hen. IV., iv. 5. 76.</poem>}}
{{smaller block|<poem>
The ladies sought around
For ''virtuous'' herbs, which, gather’d from the ground,
They squeez’d the juice and cooling ointment made.
</poem>
{{right|''Dryden'', Flower and Leaf, l. 418.}}}}
='''Syn. 2''' and '''3.''' Upright, exemplary, worthy, righteous. See ''morality''.

'''virtuously''' (vėr′tṳ̄-us-li), ''adv.'' In a virtuous manner; in conformity with the moral law or with duty; chastely; honorably.
{{smaller block|The gods are my witnesses I desire to do ''virtuously''.
{{right|''Sir P. Sidney.''}}
I knew you lov’d her, ''virtuously'' you lov’d her.
{{right|''Beau. and Fl.'', Knight of Malta, ii. 2.}}
<poem>
And I’ll be your true servant,
Ever from this hour ''virtuously'' to love you,
Chastely and modestly to look upon you.
</poem>
{{right|''Fletcher'', Rule a Wife, v. 5.}}}}

'''virtuousness''' (vėr′tṳ̄-us-nes), ''n.'' [Early mod. E. also ''vertuousnes''; < ''virtuous'' + ''-ness''.] The state or character of being virtuous.
{{smaller block|Polemon . . . from thensforthe becam a Phi’er [philosopher] of singular gravitee, of incomparable sobrenes, of moste constante ''vertuousnes'', and so contynued all his lif aftir.
{{right|''Udall'' (Ellis’s Lit. Letters, p. 6).}}

'''virulence''' (vir′ọ̈-le̤ns), ''n.'' [< F. ''virulence'' = Sp. Pg. ''virulencia'' = It. ''virulenza'', < LL. ''virulentia'', an offensive odor, < L. ''virulentus'', full of poison: see ''virulent''.] The quality of being virulent, or charged with virus. {{smaller|(''a'') The quality or property of being extremely acrimonious or poisonous: as, the ''viru-''}}<noinclude><references/></noinclude>
